newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: CURLING-CANADIAN CURLERS LOOK FOR OLYMPIC SWEEP.
newsitem.headline: CURLING-CANADIAN CURLERS LOOK FOR OLYMPIC SWEEP.

text.p: To most of the world, curling is something you impose on your hair.
For Canadians, particularly those living on the country's vast Prairies, it is something to help endure the long winters.
And it is something Canadians do particularly well.

At the world curling championships at the weekend, Sandra Schmirler guided Canada to their fourth title in five years with an 8-4 win over Norway, becoming the first women's rink to claim three world titles.
Canadian rinks had also dominated the men's competition until Friday's semifinals when Kevin Martin's Edmonton rink was upset by Sweden snapping a string of four consecutive titles.

Martin's rink also lost the bronze medal contest to Scotland, marking the first time since 1984 and only the fourth since the championships began in 1959, that a men's Canadian rink will return home without winning at least a bronze medal.
Of the last 12 world championship gold medals up for grabs, Canadian rinks have claimed 10.
Accordingly, Canadians expect two gold medals from their curlers at the Nagano Olympics, where the sport will enjoy full medal status for the first time.
"Some countries would be happy with a bronze but in Canada we're expected to win, and if you don't then it hasn't been a success," said Jim Waite, who will coach Canada's Olympic entry.
"There's no question that whoever earns the right to represent Canada is going to face unbelievable pressure and expectations."

Curling rinks in Canada are as common as cricket pitches in England or baseball diamonds in the United States. In a country of 35 million, according to Canadian Curling Association (CCA) statistics, 1.2 million are curlers, more than the rest of the world combined.
Canada's top curlers enjoy celebrity status and are commonly known by nicknames such as Schmirler 'the Curler'.

Eddie 'the Wrench' Werenich, world champion in 1983 and 1990, created a national controversy when the Canadian Olympic Association told the Toronto fireman he was too fat and had to lose weight before they would allow him to represent Canada at the 1988 Calgary Olympics where curling was a demonstration sport.

The Canadian championships, the Brier and Tournament of Hearts, are shown on live national television and traditionally attract large crowds to the arenas, a record 17,024 turning out for the men's final in Edmonton earlier this year.

"The big difference between us and other countries is that we have over a million players to choose from in Canada," said Schmirler. "In Regina alone we probably have more players than some countries here."
While curling is played across Canada, it is in the Prairie provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta where the sport flourishes.
"It's cold, there's nothing else to do," joked Jan Betker, a member of the three times world championship foursome.
Curling is more than a sport on the Prairies, it's a way of life woven into the fabric of the hundreds of farming communities where it is as much a social activity as a sport.
Three out of four members on Schmirler's Regina rink met their husbands through curling and most of their friends.
"The thing about curling is that it's a lifetime sport it's something you can play forever," said Schmirler. "In Canada you meet your friends curling, your boyfriends and your spouses.
"It becomes more than a game to people, it becomes a lifestyle."
The team disbanded for the 1995-96 season while Betker, Joan McCusker and Marcia Gudereit had babies.
Schmirler, who won her most recent title while she was five months pregnant, will have her first child in August and then immediately begin preparing for the Canadian Olympic team trials in November.
"Nothing was actually planned, the curling gods were looking out for us," laughed Schmirler. "It was just time to get on with life.
"We had spent 1993, 1994 and 1995 where curling was our main focus and it was time to get on with things.
"It's been positive for us because it's given everyone the perspective that there's more to life than curling.
"It's been an opportunity to come back and feel comfortable playing the game and not feel there were a whole bunch of things left undone at home." .
